bottarga.name: Bottarga (avgotaraho)
bottarga.summary: Salted, cured fish roe, typically from grey mullet or bluefin tuna, prepared in various cultures and regarded as an expensive delicacy.

moustalevria.name: Moustalevria
moustalevria.summary: A traditional Greek pudding made by boiling grape must with flour until thick, one of several foods traced back to Byzantine times.

paximathia.name: Paximathia
paximathia.summary: A hard, twice-baked Greek bread made from whole wheat, chickpea or barley flour, similar to rusk or biscotti, often eaten with marmalade or cheese.

alexander-kazhdan.name: Alexander Kazhdan
alexander-kazhdan.summary: A Soviet and American historian of Byzantium (1922–1997) who published the three-volume Oxford Dictionary of Byzantium, a major encyclopedia of the field.

giles-constable.name: Giles Constable
giles-constable.summary: English historian and medievalist (1929 to 2021) focused on 11th and 12th century religion and culture, especially the abbey of Cluny.

garum.name: Garum (garos)
garum.summary: A fermented fish sauce condiment used across the ancient Mediterranean world, in earlier use among the Greeks before becoming popular in Rome, with a taste compared to modern Asian fish sauces.

tarhana.name: Tarhana
tarhana.summary: A dried fermented food made from grain and yogurt or milk, found across Central Asian, Southeast European and Middle Eastern cuisines; known in Greek as trahanás.

byzantine-iconoclasm.name: Byzantine Iconoclasm
byzantine-iconoclasm.summary: Two periods (about 726–787 and 814–842) when Byzantine religious and imperial authorities opposed the veneration of icons, causing civil wars and destruction of religious images.

saint-catherine-s-monastery.name: Saint Catherine's Monastery
saint-catherine-s-monastery.summary: Christian monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai, Egypt, built 548 to 565 under Byzantine emperor Justinian I; the world's oldest continuously inhabited Christian monastery.

paris-psalter.name: Paris Psalter
paris-psalter.summary: A Byzantine illuminated manuscript with 14 full-page miniatures, considered a key work of the 10th-century Macedonian Renaissance's revival of classical art.

pliska.name: Pliska
pliska.summary: The first capital of the First Bulgarian Empire, founded in the late 7th century and later sacked by Byzantine forces in 811 before being rebuilt.

veliki-preslav.name: Preslav
veliki-preslav.summary: Capital of the First Bulgarian Empire from 893 to 972 and one of medieval Southeastern Europe's most important cities; its ruins lie in modern northeastern Bulgaria.

murfatlar-cave-complex.name: Murfatlar Cave Complex
murfatlar-cave-complex.summary: A medieval Christian monastery carved into rock near Murfatlar, Romania, a remnant of a widespread 10th-century Bulgarian monastic tradition.

simeon-i-of-bulgaria.name: Simeon I of Bulgaria
simeon-i-of-bulgaria.summary: Ruler of the First Bulgarian Empire from 893 to 927 whose campaigns brought Bulgaria to its greatest territorial extent and a golden age of culture.

tomislav-king-of-croatia.name: Tomislav
tomislav-king-of-croatia.summary: First king of Croatia, reigning from about 925 to 928, who allied with the Byzantine Empire and won a decisive battle against Bulgaria in 926.

dinaric-alps.name: Dinaric Alps
dinaric-alps.summary: A mountain range stretching about 645 km through Southern and South-Central Europe, separating the Balkan Peninsula from the Adriatic Sea.

zaharija-of-serbia.name: Zaharija
zaharija-of-serbia.summary: Ruler of Serbia from 921 to about 925/926, installed by the Byzantines and later by Bulgaria, who fled to Croatia when a larger Bulgarian army invaded.

principality-of-serbia-early-medieval.name: Principality of Serbia
principality-of-serbia-early-medieval.summary: An early medieval Serbian state ruled by the Vlastimirović dynasty from the 8th century, annexed by Bulgaria in 924 and later by the Byzantine Empire around 969 to 971.

presian-of-bulgaria.name: Presian I
presian-of-bulgaria.summary: Khan of the First Bulgarian Empire from 836 to 852 who expanded its territory westward to the Adriatic Sea, annexing much of Macedonia.

vlastimir.name: Vlastimir
vlastimir.summary: Prince of Serbia from about 830 to 851 who defeated an invading Bulgarian army in a three-year war and expanded into Dalmatia; founder of the Vlastimirović dynasty, Serbia's first dynasty.

vladimir-of-bulgaria.name: Vladimir-Rasate
vladimir-of-bulgaria.summary: Ruler of the First Bulgarian Empire from 889 to 893.

boris-i-of-bulgaria.name: Boris I of Bulgaria
boris-i-of-bulgaria.summary: Ruler of the First Bulgarian Empire from 852 to 889 who Christianized Bulgaria in 864, secured an independent Bulgarian Church, and is venerated as a saint.

mutimir-of-serbia.name: Mutimir of Serbia
mutimir-of-serbia.summary: Prince of the first Serbian Principality from about 850 to 891, who defeated a Bulgar army and allied with the Byzantine emperor and church.

aslav.name: Časlav
aslav.summary: Ruler of Serbia from about 927/928 to possibly 943/944, who escaped Bulgarian captivity and consolidated power with Byzantine help.

vlastimirovi-dynasty.name: Vlastimirović dynasty
vlastimirovi-dynasty.summary: The first Serbian royal dynasty, named after Prince Vlastimir, ruling from the early 7th century until the Byzantine Empire annexed Serbian lands in the 940s/960s.

sclaveni.name: Sclaveni
sclaveni.summary: Early Slavic tribes who raided and settled in Southeastern Europe during the Early Middle Ages, ancestors of modern South Slavs, later coming under Byzantine or Frankish rule.

constantine-vii.name: Constantine VII
constantine-vii.summary: Byzantine emperor of the Macedonian dynasty from 913 to 959, whose reign was largely dominated by co-regents and who is remembered for scholarly works describing the empire's peoples and administration.

pribislav-of-serbia.name: Pribislav
pribislav-of-serbia.summary: Prince of the Serbs for one year, 891 to 892, before his cousin Petar deposed him; eldest son of Mutimir, whose reign saw Serbia's expansion and Christianization.

stefan-mutimirovi.name: Stefan Mutimirović
stefan-mutimirovi.summary: A 9th-century Serbian royal of the ruling Vlastimirović dynasty, the younger son of Prince Mutimir.

vojvodina.name: Vojvodina
vojvodina.summary: An autonomous province in northern Serbia covering Bačka, Banat, Syrmia, and part of Mačva, with about 1.7 million people and its centre at Novi Sad.

foederati.name: Foederati
foederati.summary: Peoples, cities or barbarian groups bound to Rome by treaty, who received benefits in exchange for military help and, especially under the empire, were often allowed to settle within its borders.

heraclius.name: Heraclius
heraclius.summary: Byzantine emperor from 610 to 641 who seized power in a revolt against Phocas, then fought long wars against Persia and the Arabs, driving the Persians from Asia Minor before losing territory to Arab conquests.

basileus.name: Basileus
basileus.summary: A Greek title meaning king or emperor, used by ancient Greek rulers, Byzantine emperors and later kings of Greece; it is also the source of the name Basil.

john-malalas.name: John Malalas
john-malalas.summary: Byzantine chronicler from Antioch in Asia Minor, who lived from around 491 to 578.

theophanes-the-confessor.name: Theophanes the Confessor
theophanes-the-confessor.summary: A Byzantine aristocrat turned monk and chronicler (c. 759–817/818) who attended the Second Council of Nicaea in 787 and was imprisoned for resisting iconoclasm.

koine-greek.name: Koine Greek
koine-greek.summary: The common form of Greek spoken and written across the Hellenistic world, Roman Empire and early Byzantine Empire, spreading after Alexander the Great's conquests and used for the Septuagint and New Testament.

corpus-juris-civilis.name: Corpus Juris Civilis
corpus-juris-civilis.summary: A compilation of Roman law enacted 529-534 CE under Emperor Justinian I, made up of a legal code, a jurists' encyclopedia, and a student textbook, all given the force of law.

antikythera-mechanism.name: Antikythera mechanism
antikythera-mechanism.summary: An ancient Greek analogue-computer device built in the 2nd century BC to predict astronomical positions and eclipses, discovered in a shipwreck in 1901.

isidore-of-miletus.name: Isidore of Miletus
isidore-of-miletus.summary: A Byzantine Greek mathematician and architect born around 475 AD, commissioned with Anthemius of Tralles by Emperor Justinian I to design Constantinople's Hagia Sophia between 532 and 537.

archimedes.name: Archimedes
archimedes.summary: Ancient Greek mathematician, physicist and engineer from Syracuse (c. 287–212 BC), regarded as one of the greatest mathematicians of all time for his work on geometry, levers and buoyancy.

archimedes-palimpsest.name: Archimedes Palimpsest
archimedes-palimpsest.summary: A Byzantine manuscript compiling works of Archimedes, including two otherwise-lost texts, first assembled around AD 530 and rediscovered by scholars in 1899.

al-biruni.name: Al-Biruni
al-biruni.summary: Iranian polymath of the Islamic Golden Age (c. 973-1050) who served the Ghaznavids as a historian and court astrologer and wrote a landmark work on India around 1030.

cyril-and-methodius.name: Cyril and Methodius
cyril-and-methodius.summary: Byzantine Christian brothers (826–869 and 815–885) known as the 'Apostles to the Slavs' for devising the Glagolitic alphabet and evangelizing the early Slavic peoples.

justinian-i.name: Justinian I
justinian-i.summary: Roman emperor from 527 to 565 whose generals reconquered much of the former Western Roman Empire and who is remembered for his sweeping rewrite of Roman law.

first-bulgarian-empire.name: First Bulgarian Empire
first-bulgarian-empire.summary: Medieval Bulgarian state founded in 680–681 by Bulgars under Asparuh, which by the 9th and 10th centuries rivaled the Byzantine Empire and adopted Christianity in 864.

asparuh-of-bulgaria.name: Asparuh
asparuh-of-bulgaria.summary: A Bulgar khan of the later 7th century credited with founding the First Bulgarian Empire in 681.

constantine-iv.name: Constantine IV
constantine-iv.summary: Byzantine emperor from 668 to 685 who halted decades of Arab expansion, successfully defended Constantinople, and ended the monothelitism controversy through the Sixth Ecumenical Council.

byzantines.name: Rhomaioi (Byzantines)
byzantines.summary: The Greek name Byzantines used for themselves, meaning "Romans"; they kept this Roman identity even after Constantinople fell and they came under Ottoman rule.

siege-of-constantinople-717-718.name: Siege of Constantinople (717–718)
siege-of-constantinople-717-718.summary: A failed 717–718 siege of Byzantine Constantinople by the Umayyad Caliphate's Arab forces, broken by Byzantine naval power, harsh winter, and Bulgar attacks on the besiegers.

theophilos-emperor.name: Theophilos
theophilos-emperor.summary: Byzantine Emperor from 829 to 842, the last to support iconoclasm; he fought the Abbasid Caliphate and secured nominal overlordship over the Principality of Serbia.

krum.name: Krum
krum.summary: Khan of the First Bulgarian Empire (c. 796/803–814) whose reign doubled Bulgaria's territory and produced its first known written law code.

suda.name: Suda
suda.summary: A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world with about 30,000 entries, many preserving material from ancient sources that have since been lost.

catepanate-of-ras.name: Catepanate of Ras
catepanate-of-ras.summary: A short-lived Byzantine province established around 971 in central Serbia, named after the fortified town of Ras, which collapsed after Bulgaria's empire was restored.

nikephoros-i.name: Nikephoros I
nikephoros-i.summary: Byzantine emperor from 802 to 811 who overthrew Empress Irene to seize the throne and was killed in 811 invading Bulgaria at the Battle of Pliska.

royal-frankish-annals.name: Royal Frankish Annals
royal-frankish-annals.summary: A Latin, year-by-year chronicle of the Frankish monarchy from 741 to 829, written by authors close to the court and a key, if biased, source on Charlemagne's reign.

radoslav-of-serbia.name: Radoslav of Serbia
radoslav-of-serbia.summary: An early 9th-century prince of the Principality of Serbia who succeeded his father Višeslav and was succeeded by his son Prosigoj, ruling during a period of peace with Bulgaria.

second-council-of-nicaea.name: Second Council of Nicaea
second-council-of-nicaea.summary: A 787 CE church council that restored the veneration of icons after their suppression by Byzantine emperors, ruling that honor to an icon passes to its subject rather than the image itself.

bogomilism.name: Bogomilism
bogomilism.summary: A Christian dualist sect founded in the First Bulgarian Empire in the 10th century that rejected church hierarchy and spread through the Balkans and Byzantine Empire.

bogomil-priest.name: Bogomil
bogomil-priest.summary: A 10th-century Bulgarian priest, active during the reign of Peter I of Bulgaria, whose preaching gave rise to the Bogomilism sect; little else is known of his life.

peter-i-of-bulgaria.name: Peter I of Bulgaria
peter-i-of-bulgaria.summary: Emperor of Bulgaria from 927 to 969 who faced rebellions and the rise of Bogomilism, but whose reign is now seen as one of affluence and internal peace.

kutmichevitsa.name: Kutmichevitsa
kutmichevitsa.summary: An administrative region of the Bulgarian Empire in the 9th–11th centuries, covering parts of modern Macedonia and Albania, important to the development of Old Church Slavonic culture.

glagolitic-script.name: Glagolitic script
glagolitic-script.summary: The oldest-known Slavic alphabet, created in the 9th century by the monk Cyril to translate Greek scripture into Old Church Slavonic, later largely replaced by Cyrillic.

old-church-slavonic.name: Old Church Slavonic
old-church-slavonic.summary: The first Slavic literary language, standardized by 9th-century missionaries Cyril and Methodius for translating scripture, and ancestor of the liturgical Church Slavonic still used today.

theodore-the-studite.name: Theodore the Studite
theodore-the-studite.summary: Byzantine Greek monk and abbot (759–826) who revived monasticism and classical learning and was a fierce opponent of iconoclasm.

monastery-of-stoudios.name: Monastery of Stoudios
monastery-of-stoudios.summary: A Byzantine Greek Orthodox monastery in Constantinople founded in 462, whose monastic rules and customs became models for monasteries across the Orthodox world.

typikon.name: Typikon
typikon.summary: Liturgical book setting out the order of services and variable hymns of the Byzantine Rite.

mount-athos.name: Mount Athos
mount-athos.summary: Mountain and self-governing monastic region in Greece, a major center of Eastern Orthodox monastic life since at least the 9th century.

photios-i-of-constantinople.name: Photios I of Constantinople
photios-i-of-constantinople.summary: Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from 858 to 867 and 877 to 886 (c. 815–893), regarded as the most important intellectual of his era and a central figure in the conversion of the Slavs to Christianity.

constantine-v.name: Constantine V
constantine-v.summary: Byzantine emperor from 741 to 775, an able military leader against Arabs and Bulgars whose fervent support for iconoclasm earned him mocking nicknames from later writers.

council-of-hieria.name: Council of Hieria
council-of-hieria.summary: A 754 Christian council that condemned the veneration of religious icons as idolatrous, reflecting Byzantine emperor Constantine V's iconoclasm; the Second Council of Nicaea overturned it 33 years later.

leo-iv-the-khazar.name: Leo IV the Khazar
leo-iv-the-khazar.summary: Byzantine emperor from 775 to 780, son of Constantine V, who in 778 defeated an Abbasid army near Germanikeia; he died of tuberculosis, succeeded by his young son Constantine VI under Irene's regency.

irene-of-athens.name: Irene of Athens
irene-of-athens.summary: Byzantine empress consort from 775, later regent and co-ruler, and finally sole ruling empress of the Byzantine Empire from 797 to 802; she restored the veneration of icons despite her husband's iconoclasm.

leo-vi-the-wise.name: Leo VI the Wise
leo-vi-the-wise.summary: Byzantine emperor from 886 to 912, of the Macedonian dynasty, known for continuing a literary renaissance despite military defeats against Bulgaria and the Arabs, and for ending several ancient Roman institutions.

mirrors-for-princes.name: Mirrors for princes
mirrors-for-princes.summary: A genre of instructional books on governance and behavior for monarchs, popular from antiquity through the Renaissance; Machiavelli's The Prince is its best-known example.

ohrid.name: Ohrid
ohrid.summary: A city in North Macedonia on Lake Ohrid, once known for having 365 churches and called the "Jerusalem of the Balkans".

clement-of-ohrid.name: Clement of Ohrid
clement-of-ohrid.summary: Medieval Bulgarian scholar and saint (c. 830–916), a leading disciple of Cyril and Methodius linked to spreading the Glagolitic and Cyrillic scripts among Slavs.

medieval-greek.name: Byzantine Greek
medieval-greek.summary: The stage of the Greek language used from the end of classical antiquity until the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453, and the sole language of Byzantine administration from the 7th century on.

plague-of-justinian.name: Plague of Justinian
plague-of-justinian.summary: A pandemic (541–549 AD) that struck the Mediterranean, Europe and the Near East, killing about a fifth of Constantinople's population at its height under Emperor Justinian I.

balkan-danubian-culture.name: Balkan–Danubian culture
balkan-danubian-culture.summary: An early medieval archaeological culture of the Lower Danube region, roughly 8th to 11th centuries, known as Pliska-Preslav culture in Bulgaria and Dridu culture in Romania.

palace-of-omurtag.name: Palace of Omurtag
palace-of-omurtag.summary: An archaeological site in northeastern Bulgaria identified as the fort and palace of Omurtag, ruler of the First Bulgarian Empire from 815 to 831.
